text: A network topology is the arrangement of devices and the connections between them. Bus topology connects every device to one shared cable — cheap, but a single break can take the entire network down. Ring topology connects each device to two neighbors in a closed loop, with the same single-break weakness unless the design includes redundancy.

Star topology connects every device individually to a central switch, and it's overwhelmingly what real wired networks look like today. Its advantage: one cable failing only takes down the one device on it, not the whole network. Its weakness: the central switch itself is a single point of failure, which is why production networks add redundant switches and uplinks.

Mesh topology connects devices to multiple others directly — full mesh connects every device to every other device, which provides the most redundancy but doesn't scale: a full mesh of just 10 devices needs 45 connections. Most real enterprise networks are hybrids — star at the access layer, partial mesh at the core for redundancy.

Twisted-pair copper is the dominant medium for connecting end devices — Cat5e supports up to 1 Gbps, Cat6 and Cat6a reliably push 10 Gbps. The twisting cancels electromagnetic interference between pairs. Fiber optic cable carries light instead of electrical signals, immune to that interference, reaching kilometers instead of copper's roughly 100-meter limit.
